paras: In Chapter 3 we saw that memory changes what AI can answer. Our definitions, decisions, and experiences become part of the conditions that shape the answer.
But another question appears. What should we remember?
Should we simply store everything? No.
Storing everything is not the same as creating memory.
beats.claim: Good memory is not the memory that stores the most. It is memory stored in a form that can be understood again.

paras: If everything is stored at once, finding what matters can become harder, not easier.
Humans do not remember every moment with equal weight either. Some events remain for years. Some words disappear. Some decisions are remembered because they affect many later actions.
Some experiences become the basis for understanding other experiences.
Digital systems are no different. A store where every item carries the same weight can be searched and still answer nothing, because nothing in it is distinguishable from anything else.

Suppose we want to preserve a memory about a place. There is the name of the place, an event that happened there, a person involved, a decision made at the time, and a document explaining that decision.
We could store all of it as one long piece of text.
But later it would be hard to ask what events are related to this place, what decision was made in that event, or where the evidence for that decision is.
To ask these questions we first have to distinguish the things we remember: what is a person, what is an event, what is a decision, what is a concept, and what is a record.
beats.claim: That distinction creates the structure of memory.

beats.h: Naming Is a Way of Cutting the World
paras: Calling something a concept is not merely assigning a name. It means deciding to distinguish it from something else.

If we use the concept Decision, we can tell a decision apart from an ordinary sentence. We chose B may be part of a record. But if that sentence represents an important choice, we can remember it as a decision.
Then the question changes. We are no longer only searching for a sentence. We can search for the decision, and from it follow the reasons, evidence, and related records.
A concept is not a folder for storing memory.
beats.claim: It is an agreement about what we regard as one meaningful object.

paras: As these distinctions accumulate, a structure emerges. There are people, events, decisions, documents, and concepts. And they have relationships.
A person makes a decision. An event triggers a decision. A document explains a decision. One decision can lead to another.
At this point we have more than a list of individual concepts. We have a model of what exists and what kinds of relationships those things can have.

Ontology does not mean all the content stored in Vinc, and it is not a giant dictionary attempting to classify all of reality. It is the basic agreement of distinctions and relationships used to structure memory.

beats.h: Concepts and Records Are Not the Same
paras: A concept can serve as a durable reference for what we mean. A record is evidence actually preserved at a particular point in time.
Suppose a team uses the concept canonical source. There may be an explanation of it, and there may also be documents and decisions where it was applied in an actual project.
The concept stabilizes meaning. The record preserves the trace of that meaning being used.
Distinguishing the two makes something important possible: we can remember both the meaning we use now and the original record that supports it.
beats.claim: An AI can answer about a concept and still follow it back to where the definition came from.

paras: Not all records carry the same kind of memory. Decisions in particular keep affecting us long after they were made.
Remembering only that we chose B is different from remembering why we chose B. And if the decision was later changed, that change needs to be remembered too.
Otherwise an old decision can be mistaken for a current rule.
So time matters for decisions. When was it made? What supported it? Is it still valid? Why was it changed?
A rule that has quietly expired still reads exactly like a rule that holds.
beats.claim: Memory preserves not only an old answer, but when and why that answer was valid.

beats.h: When Structure Appears, the Graph Comes Alive
paras: In Chapter 3 we said a graph preserves relationships between memories. Now the reason is clearer.
To build a graph we first have to decide what counts as a node and what counts as a relationship. Ontology provides that basis.
A graph is not merely a technology for drawing lines. Its structure contains the distinctions we made about what is worth remembering, and the relationships we judged meaningful.
The graph is the form of memory. Ontology is closer to the language and the agreement that creates that form.

beats.h: It Does Not Try to Explain Everything
paras: There is a temptation to classify everything in reality, and it leads to a different problem: a perfect ontology becomes a project larger than the memory system itself.
The purpose is not to reproduce reality perfectly. It is to keep the meanings we will need again from being lost.
So we distinguish only as much as necessary. A new kind of memory can be added when needed, and a distinction can stop being used when it no longer matters.
We should begin with what we may need again, what helps us understand other memories, what can be checked against evidence, and what can be traced through time.
beats.claim: Text is important evidence. What it means, and how it connects, has to be kept as well.

beats.label: 4.close
paras: We now have a structure. We distinguish what to remember, define it as concepts, connect records and decisions, and represent those relationships as a graph.
But one question remains. Whose memory is it? The moment memory begins to move beyond the individual, it needs another kind of structure.
